claim: Release probability at CA3-CA1 synapses increases with greater distances from the soma.
source: We find that their release probability increases with greater distances from the soma.
evidence: Supported by optical quantal analysis data showing linear regression with p < 0.001 and Pearson's r = 0.413 (Figure 1C), and by iGluSnFR measurements showing PPR decrease with distance (Figure 3C).

claim: Similar-fidelity synapses tend to group together along dendrites.
source: Similar-fidelity synapses tend to group together, whereas release probability shows no trends regarding the branch ends.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing that percentage difference in Pr between two synapses on one dendritic branch correlates with distance between them (Figure 2B, p = 0.00987, r = 0.623).

claim: Release probability shows no trends regarding the branch ends.
source: Similar-fidelity synapses tend to group together, whereas release probability shows no trends regarding the branch ends.
evidence: Supported by data showing no significant correlation between Pr and relative synapse position at dendritic branch (Figure 2C, p = 0.176, r = 0.173).

claim: The observed Pr trends boost signal transfer fidelity, particularly at higher input frequencies.
source: Simulations with a realistic CA1 pyramidal cell hosting stochastic synapses suggest that the observed trends boost signal transfer fidelity, particularly at higher input frequencies.
evidence: Supported by NEURON model simulations showing that Pr trend improves signal transfer with effect increasing at higher frequencies (Figure 4C, D).

claim: High-frequency bursting has been associated with learning.
source: Because high-frequency bursting has been associated with learning, the release probability pattern we have found may play a key role in memory trace formation.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: The release probability pattern found may play a key role in memory trace formation.
source: Because high-frequency bursting has been associated with learning, the release probability pattern we have found may play a key role in memory trace formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of experimental findings about Pr trends and established knowledge about high-frequency bursting in learning.

claim: In hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, synaptic receptor numbers increase monotonically with the synapse-soma distance.
source: In hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, synaptic receptor numbers increase monotonically with the synapse-soma distance (Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Nicholson et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regenerative properties of local ion channels combined with increased receptor numbers can provide efficient, relatively homogeneous summation of synaptic inputs across the dendritic tree of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: This, combined with the regenerative properties of local ion channels (Cash and Yuste, 1999; Magee, 1999), can provide efficient, relatively homogeneous summation of synaptic inputs across the dendritic tree of these cells (Cash and Yuste, 1999; Magee, 2000; Magee and Cook, 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Distal synapses on cortical L5 pyramidal neurons appear relatively ineffective in somatic excitation.
source: In contrast, distal synapses on cortical L5 pyramidal neurons appear relatively ineffective in somatic excitation (Williams and Stuart, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Pr defines how much information synaptic connections transmit over time.
source: Because Pr defines how much information synaptic connections transmit over time (Zador, 1998), its distribution pattern is critical to the rules of dendritic input integration.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: The distribution pattern of Pr is critical to the rules of dendritic input integration.
source: Because Pr defines how much information synaptic connections transmit over time (Zador, 1998), its distribution pattern is critical to the rules of dendritic input integration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited relationship between Pr and information transmission.

claim: A recent study found average Pr values decreasing towards the cell periphery in basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: A recent elegant study has combined electron microscopy with extracellular (paired-pulse) afferent activation of multiple synapses in basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells, to find the average Pr values decreasing towards the cell periphery (Grillo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Individual dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal cells host almost exclusively only one CA3-CA1 synapse.
source: Because individual dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal cells host almost exclusively only one CA3-CA1 synapse (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Bloss et al., 2018), the first-pulse Ca2+ signal success counts over 14–30 trials provided direct readout of Pr at individual synapses (P1 in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), as we showed earlier (Sylantyev et al., 2013; Boddum et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The first-pulse Ca2+ signal success counts over 14-30 trials provided direct readout of Pr at individual synapses.
source: Because individual dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal cells host almost exclusively only one CA3-CA1 synapse (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Bloss et al., 2018), the first-pulse Ca2+ signal success counts over 14–30 trials provided direct readout of Pr at individual synapses (P1 in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), as we showed earlier (Sylantyev et al., 2013; Boddum et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous methodological studies and current experimental data.

claim: Average release probability (Pr) at individual synapses was 0.36 ± 0.02 (mean ± SEM).
source: A systematic application of this protocol at n = 67 individual synapses (53 cells) has revealed a highly significant trend towards higher Pr at more distal synapses (Figure 1C), with average Pr = 0.36 ± 0.02 (mean ± SEM).
evidence: Directly measured from experimental data across 67 synapses.

claim: Linear regression for Pr vs distance data suggested a rise in average Pr from ~0.2 at 50 µm to ~0.5 at 300 µm.
source: The linear regression for the data suggested a rise in average Pr from ~0.2 at 50 µm to ~0.5 at 300 µm (range 0.05–0.7; Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on linear regression analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio of release probabilities decreased, on average, from ~3 to ~1.1 over the distance range of 50-300 µm.
source: Over this distance range, the PPR of release probabilities decreased, on average, from ~3 to ~1.1, for either P2 or P2* counts (Figure 1D–E; experiments with no reliable 2nd response detection and no 'failure-success' responses were not included).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: An earlier report detected no distance-dependent Pr trends along apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells using MK801-based approach.
source: There observations appear at variance with an elegant earlier report which detected no distance-dependent Pr trends along apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells, based on the use-dependent blockade of NMDARs by MK801 (Smith et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The MK801-based approach is sensitive to local glutamate spillover.
source: However, the MK801-based approach is sensitive to local glutamate spillover (Scimemi et al., 2004) and, in that case, involved a Mg2+-free solution, both of which could mask the Pr trend.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A previous study documented 15-50% lower average PPR values in distal compared to proximal synapses, consistently over 25-200 ms paired-pulse intervals, albeit without reaching statistical significance in a six-cell sample.
source: Intriguingly, that study documented 15–50% lower average PPR values in distal compared to proximal synapses, consistently over 25–200 ms paired-pulse intervals, albeit without reaching statistical significance in a six-cell sample (Smith et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The centrifugal trend in Pr values remained significant when the distance was measured from the primary apical dendrites.
source: The centrifugal trend in Pr values remained significant when the distance was measured from the primary apical dendrites (Figure 2A), suggesting that this trend applies to oblique branches rather than simply reflecting a position along the main dendrite.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A with p = 0.00231, r = 0.378.

claim: The Pr trend applies to oblique branches rather than simply reflecting a position along the main dendrite.
source: The centrifugal trend in Pr values remained significant when the distance was measured from the primary apical dendrites (Figure 2A), suggesting that this trend applies to oblique branches rather than simply reflecting a position along the main dendrite.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the trend persists when measured from primary dendrites.

claim: Connections with similar Pr tend to occur close to one another on the same dendrite.
source: Interestingly, the analysis of Pr values recorded in pairs of synapses located on the same dendrite has revealed that the connections with similar Pr tend to occur close to one another (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with p = 0.00987, r = 0.623.

claim: Homogenisation of Pr among local synapses was detected previously in cultured neurons.
source: Thus, 'homogenisation' of Pr among local synapses, which was detected previously in cultured neurons (Branco et al., 2008), is likely to occur in ex vivo brain tissue.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Homogenisation of Pr among local synapses is likely to occur in ex vivo brain tissue.
source: Thus, 'homogenisation' of Pr among local synapses, which was detected previously in cultured neurons (Branco et al., 2008), is likely to occur in ex vivo brain tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on current experimental findings combined with previous observations in cultured neurons.

claim: There were no trends in Pr values with respect to the synapse position relative to the local dendrite branching point.
source: At the same time, we found no trends in Pr values with respect to the synapse position relative to the local dendrite branching point (Figure 2C; the centrifugal Pr trend in these data does not reach statistical significance because branch length is much smaller than the overall dendritic length, thus providing much reduced statistical power).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with p = 0.176, r = 0.173.

claim: The prevalence of larger, more densely packed spines near the dendritic branch origins was earlier reported to reflect normalisation of synaptic signals integrated at the soma.
source: The prevalence of larger, more densely packed spines near the dendritic branch origins was earlier reported to reflect normalisation of synaptic signals integrated at the soma (Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: No gradient in Pr values within a branch suggests that normalisation of synaptic signals should still be valid during sustained afferent activity.
source: In this context, no gradient in Pr values within a branch (Figure 2C) suggests that the above normalisation should still be valid during sustained afferent activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental finding of no Pr gradient within branches.

claim: Higher Pr are normally associated with lower PPRs.
source: Because higher Pr are normally associated with lower PPRs (as in Figure 1D), the probability of both stimuli initiating successful release showed only a barely detectable increase with the spine-soma distance (Figure 2D), whereas the second-release Pr values were evenly spread along the dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge in synaptic physiology, supported by the current data in Figure 1D.

claim: The probability of both stimuli initiating successful release showed only a barely detectable increase with the spine-soma distance.
source: Because higher Pr are normally associated with lower PPRs (as in Figure 1D), the probability of both stimuli initiating successful release showed only a barely detectable increase with the spine-soma distance (Figure 2D), whereas the second-release Pr values were evenly spread along the dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The second-release Pr values were evenly spread along the dendrites.
source: Because higher Pr are normally associated with lower PPRs (as in Figure 1D), the probability of both stimuli initiating successful release showed only a barely detectable increase with the spine-soma distance (Figure 2D), whereas the second-release Pr values were evenly spread along the dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The longitudinal density of optically identifiable dendritic spines increased towards distal dendrites.
source: However, the longitudinal density of optically identifiable dendritic spines increased towards distal dendrites (Figure 2E), also showing positive correlation with the Pr (Figure 2F), but no correlation with the PPR values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E with p = 0.0207, r = 0.286.

claim: Spine density showed positive correlation with Pr.
source: However, the longitudinal density of optically identifiable dendritic spines increased towards distal dendrites (Figure 2E), also showing positive correlation with the Pr (Figure 2F), but no correlation with the PPR values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F with p = 0.0460, r = 0.245.

claim: Spine density showed no correlation with PPR values.
source: However, the longitudinal density of optically identifiable dendritic spines increased towards distal dendrites (Figure 2E), also showing positive correlation with the Pr (Figure 2F), but no correlation with the PPR values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Patterns of release probability at CA3-CA1 synapses can be successfully gauged by monitoring presynaptic glutamate release with the genetically encoded optical sensor iGluSnFR.
source: We have previously shown (Jensen et al., 2017; Jensen et al., 2019) that the patterns of release probability at CA3-CA1 synapses can be successfully gauged by monitoring presynaptic glutamate release with the genetically encoded optical sensor iGluSnFR (Marvin et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: In iGluSnFR recordings with extracellular stimulation, failures could not be reliably detected throughout the trials.
source: It turned out that in such recordings we could not reliably detect failures, throughout the trials (examples in Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the hippocampal neuropil, released glutamate molecules can travel for up to ~2 μm from the synapse.
source: In the hippocampal neuropil, released glutamate molecules can travel for up to ~2 μm from the synapse (Armbruster et al., 2020), not necessarily entering other synaptic clefts (see Discussion).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The density of glutamatergic connections in area CA1 is ~2.0 μm−2.
source: Given the density of glutamatergic connections in area CA1 of ~2.0 μm−2 (Rusakov and Kullmann, 1998), individual synapses have >60 neighbours within the 2 μm proximity (i.e. within the spherical volume of ~33 μm3).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Individual synapses have >60 neighbours within the 2 μm proximity.
source: Given the density of glutamatergic connections in area CA1 of ~2.0 μm−2 (Rusakov and Kullmann, 1998), individual synapses have >60 neighbours within the 2 μm proximity (i.e. within the spherical volume of ~33 μm3).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the cited density value and geometric considerations.

claim: Two-photon excitation imaging collects emission signal integrated over a ~1-μm-thick focal plane.
source: Furthermore, two-photon excitation imaging collects emission signal integrated over a ~ 1-μm-thick focal plane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about two-photon microscopy.

claim: Extracellular stimulation is likely to generate an iGluSnFR fluorescence transient due to glutamate spillover even if only a small fraction of local axons gets excited.
source: Thus, extracellular stimulation is likely to generate an iGluSnFR fluorescence transient due to glutamate spillover even if only a small fraction of local axons gets excited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the density of synapses, glutamate diffusion distance, and imaging properties.

claim: The iGluSnFR signals reflect release activity of several local synapses.
source: This implies that the iGluSnFR signals reported here reflect release activity of several local synapses, which makes this approach suitable for PPR measurements rather than for direct Pr estimates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of glutamate spillover and synapse density.

claim: Measuring the amplitudes of paired-pulse iGluSnFR signal transients revealed a clear trend towards lower PPR with greater distances from the s. pyramidale.
source: Measuring the amplitudes of paired-pulse iGluSnFR signal transients thus revealed a clear trend towards lower PPR, hence higher Pr values, with greater distances from the s. pyramidale (PPR mean ± SEM: 1.49 ± 0.01, n = 33; regression at p<0.001; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with p < 0.001, r = -0.846.

claim: The iGluSnFR PPR data were qualitatively consistent with the PPR data obtained with the OQA of Ca2+ signals.
source: This observation was qualitatively consistent with the PPR data obtained with the OQA of Ca2+ signals (Figure 1D-E) .
evidence: This is a comparison between two different experimental approaches in the current study.

claim: The first iGluSnFR response amplitude showed no distance dependence.
source: In contrast, the first iGluSnFR response amplitude on its own showed no distance dependence (ΔF/F0, mean ± SEM: 37 ± 0.5%; range 0.18–0.81; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The iGluSnFR signal amplitude depends on several poorly controlled local concomitants, such as the degree of glutamate spillover and/or density of activated axons.
source: The latter was expected because, in addition to Pr per se, the iGluSnFR signal amplitude depends on several poorly controlled local concomitants, such as the degree of glutamate spillover (which in turn depends on the local expression of iGluSnFR and glutamate transporters) and/or density of activated axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of the factors affecting iGluSnFR signals.

claim: The slope of linear regression among five ΔF/F0 peak points increased significantly with greater distances to the s. pyramidale.
source: Intriguingly, the slope values increased significantly with greater distances to the s. pyramidale (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting greater fidelity in signal transfer by spike bursts towards more distal dendrites, as further explored below.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C with p < 0.001, r = 0.641.

claim: The slope data suggest greater fidelity in signal transfer by spike bursts towards more distal dendrites.
source: Intriguingly, the slope values increased significantly with greater distances to the s. pyramidale (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting greater fidelity in signal transfer by spike bursts towards more distal dendrites, as further explored below.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental slope data.

claim: An earlier study used simulations with a sphere-and-cylinder cell model to understand how uneven distribution of Pr values affects signal handling by the postsynaptic cell.
source: To understand how the uneven distribution of Pr values affects signal handling by the postsynaptic cell, an earlier study used simulations with a sphere-and-cylinder cell model (Grillo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The Pr trend adds ~13% to the single-pulse EPSP amplitude while decreasing PPR by ~20%, compared to the evenly distributed Pr.
source: The results show that the Pr trend, on average, adds ~13% to the single-pulse EPSP amplitude while decreasing PPR by ~20%, compared to the evenly distributed Pr, whereas adding the density trend produces little further change (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by NEURON model simulation results shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Adding the density trend produces little further change to EPSP amplitude and PPR beyond the Pr trend alone.
source: The results show that the Pr trend, on average, adds ~13% to the single-pulse EPSP amplitude while decreasing PPR by ~20%, compared to the evenly distributed Pr, whereas adding the density trend produces little further change (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by NEURON model simulation results shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The Pr trend, when combined with the five-pulse slope trend, boosts the voltage transfer value during burst activity by ~15%.
source: Qualitatively similar results were obtained for the five-pulse burst tests based on the iGluSnFR data, suggesting that the Pr trend, when combined with the five-pulse slope trend (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), boosts the voltage transfer value during the burst activity by ~15% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The main role of Pr in synaptic signal integration and transfer is played out when a time series of afferent spikes generate a postsynaptic spiking response.
source: However, the main role of Pr in synaptic signal integration and transfer is played out when a time series of afferent spikes, rather than one synchronous discharge, generate a postsynaptic spiking response (Thomson, 2000; Williams and Stuart, 2002; Williams and Atkinson, 2007; Grillo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Relatively intense synaptic input activity seen in pyramidal cells in vivo could correspond to a relatively low spiking frequency at the individual multiple afferents converging onto these cells.
source: Thus, relatively intense synaptic input activity seen in pyramidal cells in vivo could correspond to a relatively low spiking frequency at the individual multiple afferents converging onto these cells (Bähner et al., 2011; Kowalski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and logical inference.

claim: Short-term plasticity of intense synaptic input is actually driven mainly by the evolution of Pr values over low or moderate spiking frequencies at individual axons.
source: These considerations suggest that short-term plasticity, if any, of intense synaptic input is actually driven mainly by the evolution of Pr values over low or moderate spiking frequencies at individual axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between individual axon firing rates and overall synaptic input.

claim: Having the Pr trend provides a clear advantage for signal transfer fidelity, which is particularly prominent at higher input frequencies.
source: The outcome shows that having the Pr trend provides a clear advantage for signal transfer fidelity, which is particularly prominent at higher input frequencies (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A recent study established the time-dependent degree of presynaptic short-term plasticity during afferent bursts over a wide range of firing frequencies at CA3-CA1 synapses.
source: In fact, a recent study of the CA3-CA1 circuitry has established the time-dependent degree of (presynaptic) short-term plasticity (STP) during afferent bursts, over a wide range of firing frequencies (Mukunda and Narayanan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: During repetitive presynaptic activity, Pr undergoes prominent facilitation and depression within the first 2-4 discharges, followed by a near-constant Pr value that depends on the average input frequency.
source: In brief, during repetitive presynaptic activity, Pr undergoes prominent facilitation and depression within the first 2–4 discharges, followed by a near-constant Pr value that depends on the average input frequency (Mukunda and Narayanan, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: When incorporating STP mechanism, the Pr trend improves signal transfer, with the effect monotonically increasing with higher frequencies of afferent firing.
source: Equipped with this STP mechanism, we generated Poisson-process afferent input in our model and found, once again, that the Pr trend improves signal transfer, with the effect monotonically increasing with higher frequencies of afferent firing (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Passive electric properties of neuronal dendrites impose distance-dependent attenuation of synaptic receptor current.
source: Passive electric properties of neuronal dendrites impose distance-dependent attenuation of synaptic receptor current.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Distal synapses should have a progressively weaker influence on somatic spike generation due to cable properties.
source: Thus, distal synapses should have a progressively weaker influence on somatic spike generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on established cable theory.

claim: Ion channel properties at distal dendrites enable local regenerative events.
source: However, studies in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells have found that synaptic receptor numbers increase with the synapse-soma distance (Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Nicholson et al., 2006) and that ion channel properties at distal dendrites enable local regenerative events (Cash and Yuste, 1999; Magee, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Increased receptor numbers and regenerative ion channel properties underpin near-linear summation of synaptic inputs across the entire dendritic tree of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: These features seem to underpin near-linear summation of synaptic inputs across the entire tree (Cash and Yuste, 1999; Magee, 2000; Magee and Cook, 2000), thus rescuing the efficiency of dendritic signal integration.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Equal contribution of individual axo-dendritic synapses to somatic signal assumes that their average discharge rates are similar.
source: However, equal contribution of individual axo-dendritic synapses to somatic signal assumes that their average discharge rates are similar.
evidence: This is a logical inference about synaptic integration.

claim: Average discharge rates of synapses directly depend on Pr and its use-dependent plasticity.
source: This in turn directly depends on Pr and its use-dependent plasticity at individual synapses (Williams and Stuart, 2002; Williams and Atkinson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OQA requires only single-pulse stimulation and establishes absolute, rather than relative, Pr values.
source: Firstly, OQA requires only single-pulse stimulation and establishes absolute, rather than relative, Pr values and their distribution pattern along the dendrites.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage of the OQA approach.

claim: OQA deals with confirmed afferent activation of individual synapses and thus avoids the potential dependence between excitability of an axon and Pr value at its synapses.
source: Secondly, OQA deals with confirmed afferent activation of individual synapses and thus avoids the potential dependence between excitability of an axon and Pr value at its synapses, which would be masked in multiple-fibre stimulation.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage of the OQA approach.

claim: Intrinsic differences in the short-term plasticity kinetics among different synaptic populations may contribute to the variation in PPRs.
source: Thirdly, intrinsic differences in the short-term plasticity kinetics among different synaptic populations may contribute to the variation in PPRs.
evidence: This is a consideration about factors affecting PPR measurements.

claim: The progressive blockade of the NMDAR current by MK-801 may involve a degree of local inter-synaptic NMDAR activation via glutamate spillover.
source: As for the Pr assessment based on the use-dependent NMDA receptor blocker MK-801, the progressive blockade of the NMDAR current may involve a degree of local inter-synaptic NMDAR activation via glutamate spillover (Scimemi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The postsynaptic optical Ca2+ signal displays S-shape sensitivity to the underlying NMDAR current, making it virtually insensitive to small current increments near the bottom and top of the scale.
source: The latter should have a much smaller effect on the postsynaptic optical Ca2+ signal which, classically, displays S-shape sensitivity to the underlying NMDAR current, so, it is virtually insensitive to small current increments near the bottom (release failure) and near the top (release success) of the scale.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ca2+ signal properties.

claim: Multiple studies have indicated that postsynaptic Ca2+ signals elicited by local afferent stimuli or glutamate uncaging do not spread to neighbouring spines under suitable protocols.
source: Indeed, multiple studies involving classical OQA or single-synapse LTP induction have indicated that, under suitable protocols, postsynaptic Ca2+ signals elicited either by local afferent stimuli or by glutamate uncaging, do not spread to neighbouring spines (Oertner et al., 2002; Emptage et al., 2003; Boddum et al., 2016; Henneberger et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The main limitation of OQA is the low signal-to-noise ratio, at least at some connections.
source: The technically strenuous OQA has its own limitations, of which the main one is the low signal-to-noise ratio, at least at some connections.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on the authors' experience.

claim: High-affinity Ca2+ indicators tend to saturate rapidly, preventing reliable Pr readout for more than ~2 successive stimuli.
source: In addition, the high-affinity (slowly unbinding) Ca2+ indicators required to detect dendritic spine signals tend to saturate rapidly, thus preventing reliable Pr readout for more than ~2 successive stimuli.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on the properties of Ca2+ indicators.

claim: The sampling of synapses in OQA safely included the Pr range from 0.1 to 0.9.
source: We therefore, firstly, focused on synapses that showed a clear distinction between failures and successes (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), noting that this sampling still safely included the Pr range from 0.1 to 0.9 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Low Pearson's r between variables reflects large biological variability of Pr among synapses.
source: Indeed, the unexplained variance in the scatters, which is (1−r2), reflects large biological variability of Pr among synapses, as expected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical properties of the data.

claim: In establishing the significance of a population-average trend, prediction power of individual measurements is often irrelevant because uncertainty about the trend will diminish with sampling.
source: However, in establishing the significance of a population-average trend such prediction power is often irrelevant because the uncertainty about the trend will diminish with sampling (which would effectively cancel out the symmetrical noise around the trend).
evidence: This is a statistical reasoning about interpretation of correlation coefficients.

claim: The statistical significance of the trend (p value for the non-zero slope) is a factor of prevailing importance in the present context.
source: Thus, we must consider the statistical significance of the trend (p value for the non-zero slope) as a factor of prevailing importance, in the present context.
evidence: This is a statement about the appropriate statistical interpretation for the study design.

claim: Both classical OQA and the iGluSnFR approach point to the centrifugal increase of Pr in apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: We have thus found that both classical OQA and the iGluSnFR approach point to the centrifugal increase of Pr in apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings from two different methods.

claim: An earlier study found that at CA3-CA1 synapses release probability varies with the size of synaptic contacts.
source: Intriguingly, an earlier study has found that at CA3-CA1 synapses release probability detected with OQA varies with the size of synaptic contacts (Holderith et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The finding that Pr varies with synapse size, combined with evidence for greater AMPAR receptor numbers at more distal synapses, is fully consistent with the notion of Pr increasing with distance to the soma.
source: This finding, combined with the evidence for greater AMPAR receptor numbers at more distal synapses (Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Nicholson et al., 2006), is fully consistent with the notion of Pr increasing with the distance to the soma in these cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Synaptic organisation can powerfully compensate for the electrotonic weakness of synapses in distal dendrites.
source: Such data lend support to the idea that synaptic organisation can powerfully compensate for the 'electrotonic weakness' of synapses in distal dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The effects found are similar to the location-dependent features of synaptic inputs revealed with paired recordings between L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the neocortex.
source: The effects found here are similar to the location-dependent features of synaptic inputs revealed with paired recordings between L2/3 and L5 pyramidal neurons in the neocortex (Williams and Stuart, 2002; Williams and Atkinson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The occurrence of higher-efficacy synapses at distal dendrites must boost temporal summation of local CA3-CA1 inputs.
source: Clearly, the occurrence of the higher-efficacy synapses at distal dendrites must boost temporal summation of local CA3-CA1 inputs (Stuart and Spruston, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings, with citation to relevant review.

claim: LTP induction at distal synapses involves local sodium spikes.
source: This is consistent with the observation that LTP induction there involves local sodium spikes (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Individual CA3-CA1 axons make multiple synapses in distal (rather than proximal) dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Furthermore, it has recently been found that individual CA3-CA1 axons make multiple synapses in distal (rather than proximal) dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells (Bloss et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The finding that individual axons make multiple distal synapses argues for added efficiency of distal synaptic connections.
source: This further argues for added efficiency of distal synaptic connections, and is in line with the relatively high dendritic spine density found here.
evidence: This is an inference connecting previous findings with current observations.

claim: The spine density estimate could be affected by limited resolution of two-photon excitation imaging which may not detect smallest or thinnest spines.
source: Because the spine density estimate could be affected by limited resolution of two-photon excitation imaging (which may not necessarily detect smallest or thinnest spines), it would be prudent to assume that here we refer mainly to larger, mushroom-type dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the limitations of the imaging approach.

claim: Comparing present results with earlier findings suggests that dendritic integration traits at basal and apical inputs in CA1 pyramidal cells are starkly different.
source: Notwithstanding methodological differences, comparing the present results with the earlier findings (Grillo et al., 2018) suggests that the dendritic integration traits at basal and apical inputs in CA1 pyramidal cells are starkly different.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of current findings with previous study.

claim: Excitatory inputs to basal dendrites in the s. oriens include axons of other pyramidal cells, septal fibre, and commissural axons from the contralateral hippocampus.
source: Excitatory inputs to basal dendrites in the s. oriens include axons of other pyramidal cells, septal fibre, and commissural axons from the contralateral hippocampus.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The spine density in basal dendrites increases almost twofold away from the soma.
source: Interestingly, the spine density here increases almost twofold away from the soma (Bannister and Larkman, 1995; Ballesteros-Yáñez et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Biophysical modelling suggested that the Pr and PPR trends in basal dendrites help to facilitate supra-linear summation of local generative events such as dendritic spikes.
source: For instance, biophysical modelling of a simplified neuron suggested that the Pr and PPR trends in basal dendrites help to facilitate supra-linear summation of local generative events such as dendritic spikes (Grillo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Dendritic spikes have long been considered as a key mechanism of distal dendritic signalling.
source: Indeed, such events have long been considered as a key mechanism of distal dendritic signalling (Larkum and Nevian, 2008; Branco and Häusser, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In an intact rat brain, CA1 pyramidal cells tend to fire in short, high-frequency bursts.
source: Importantly, in an intact rat brain, CA1 pyramidal cells tend to fire in short, high-frequency bursts (Bähner et al., 2011; Kowalski et al., 2016) associated with sharp-wave ripple complexes (Bähner et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sharp-wave ripple complexes are thought to represent a powerful mechanism of memory consolidation in the hippocampus.
source: The latter type of synchronised neuronal activity is thought to represent a powerful mechanism of memory consolidation in the hippocampus (Gruart et al., 2006; Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Short bursts of activity have long been considered as a key unit of information transfer by stochastic synapses.
source: In fact, short bursts of activity have long been considered as a key unit of information transfer by stochastic synapses (Lisman, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The Pr trend found in apical dendrites must play an essential role in supporting and enhancing the cellular underpinning of learning and memory in the brain.
source: Thus, the Pr trend found here in apical dendrites must play an essential role in supporting and enhancing the cellular underpinning of learning and memory in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings combined with knowledge about burst firing and memory consolidation.

claim: Experiments were performed using 300-350 µm transverse hippocampal slices of 3- to 4-week-old rats.
source: We used 300–350 µm transverse hippocampal slices of 3- to 4-week-old rats (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental preparation.

claim: CA1 pyramidal cells were held in whole-cell mode at Vm = −65 mV and dialysed with Alexa Fluor 594 (50 µM) and Ca2+-sensitive indicators.
source: First, we held CA1 pyramidal cells in whole-cell (Vm = −65 mV) and dialysed them with the red morphological tracer Alexa Fluor 594 (50 µM) and Ca2+-sensitive indicators as detailed in Materials and methods and described previously (Sylantyev et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The extracellular stimulating pipette was placed in the 10-20 µm proximity of apical dendrites.
source: We visualised cell morphology with two-photon excitation (λx2p = 800 nm), and placed the extracellular stimulating pipette in the 10–20 µm proximity of apical dendrites (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The amplitudes of successful first-pulse release signals were consistently above two standard deviations of the average signal during release failures.
source: In these tests, the amplitudes of successful first-pulse release signals were consistently above two standard deviations of the average signal during release failures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), enabling us to readily calculate Pr = P1.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The average PPR (P2/P1) was 2.14 ± 0.17 (mean ± SEM) for n = 41 synapses.
source: (D) Paired-pulse ratio P2/P1 plotted against distance to the soma. Other notations as in (C) (n = 41; average PPR mean ± SEM: 2.14 ± 0.17; spines with no reliable detection of 2nd responses, and no detectable (0,1) responses, were excluded).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The average adjusted PPR (PPR*=P2*/P1) was 2.05 ± 0.18 (mean ± SEM) for n = 41 synapses.
source: (E) Adjusted paired-pulse ratio PPR*=P2*/P1 plotted against distance to the soma. Other notations as in (C) (n = 41; average PPR*=2.05 ± 0.18).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The average probability of the second release was 0.633 ± 0.20 (mean ± SEM) for n = 41 synapses.
source: (A) Average probability of the second release (paired-pulse stimuli 50 ms apart) plotted against distance to the soma; sample mean ± SEM: 0.633 ± 0.20 (n = 41).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The average PPR for iGluSnFR measurements was 1.49 ± 0.01 (mean ± SEM) for n = 33 boutons.
source: Measuring the amplitudes of paired-pulse iGluSnFR signal transients thus revealed a clear trend towards lower PPR, hence higher Pr values, with greater distances from the s. pyramidale (PPR mean ± SEM: 1.49 ± 0.01, n = 33; regression at p<0.001; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The average first iGluSnFR response amplitude was 37 ± 0.5% (ΔF/F0, mean ± SEM) with range 0.18-0.81.
source: In contrast, the first iGluSnFR response amplitude on its own showed no distance dependence (ΔF/F0, mean ± SEM: 37 ± 0.5%; range 0.18–0.81; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The NEURON model incorporated 50 excitatory synapses distributed over the dendritic apical tree between 40 and 350 µm from the soma.
source: Fifty synapses were distributed over the dendritic apical tree, between 40 and 350 µm from the soma, either uniformly randomly or scattered randomly in accord with the experimental statistical trend, as specified.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters.

claim: In the NEURON model, average Pr (P1) was set at 0.36 and P2 at 0.77.
source: To replicate our experimental observations of release probability, the average Pr (P1) was set at 0.36, and P2 at 0.77.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters.

claim: In simulations with the Pr trend, P1 was set as a function of synapse-soma distance x: P1 = (0.18 + 0.0012x).
source: In the case of the experimental (centrifugal) Pr trend, the Pr (P1) and P2 values were set as a function of the synapse-soma distance x: P1 = (0.18 + 0.0012x), and P2 = (0.18 + 0.0012x) ∙ (3.31–0.0074x), reflecting experimental regressions, with the average Pr value kept at 0.36 throughout, to ensure the unchanged overall efficacy of integrated synaptic input.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters based on experimental data.

claim: In simulations with the Pr trend, P2 was set as: P2 = (0.18 + 0.0012x) ∙ (3.31–0.0074x).
source: In the case of the experimental (centrifugal) Pr trend, the Pr (P1) and P2 values were set as a function of the synapse-soma distance x: P1 = (0.18 + 0.0012x), and P2 = (0.18 + 0.0012x) ∙ (3.31–0.0074x), reflecting experimental regressions, with the average Pr value kept at 0.36 throughout, to ensure the unchanged overall efficacy of integrated synaptic input.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model parameters based on experimental data.
